title: Magnetic control of nano-cerebrospinal fluid dynamics in the subarachnoid region: Neurotherapeutic applications
abstract: The dynamic behavior of nano-cerebrospinal fluid (NCSF) flow in the subarachnoid channel under external magnetic stimulation is investigated in this study, with findings aimed at advancing neurological drug delivery and treatment strategies. The Casson fluid model is employed to characterize the yield-stress behavior inherent to NCSF, enabling the simulation of transient flow within the subarachnoid space bounded by the pia and arachnoid maters. The regulating equations account for oscillatory pressure gradients, Lorentz forces due to the magnetic field, porous medium effects, and nanoparticle volume fraction. Results demonstrate that key parameters such as the Hartmann number, Darcy number, Casson parameter, and oscillation frequency significantly influence NCSF flow velocity profiles, and shear stress and volumetric flow rate distributions. Increased magnetic strength suppresses NCSF flow velocity and enhances shear stress, while higher porosity (larger Darcy number) facilitates fluid transport. The findings suggest that magnetic fields can be used to modulate NCSF flow dynamics, rendering potential strategies for improving nanoparticle-assisted drug delivery, managing conditions like hydrocephalus, and enhancing clearance of neurotoxic metabolites in neurodegenerative disorders. This work provides a theoretical foundation for novel non-invasive therapeutic interventions in neurology.

title: Realizability-constrained machine learning for turbulence closures in wake flows
authors: Talib Ansari, Priyank H. Mehta, Harshal D. Akolekar
abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-driven machine learning frameworks based on symbolic regression offer a promising pathway for turbulence model discovery, but are often hindered by numerical instability, residual stagnation, and violations of realizability during training. In particular, realizability, which is rarely enforced explicitly during model development, remains a critical yet overlooked requirement, especially for accurate wake prediction. In this work, a residual- and realizability-filtered CFD-driven framework is proposed to enhance both computational efficiency and numerical robustness within a gene expression programming (GEP) paradigm. The method integrates two residual-based filtering criteria along with a barycentric-map-based realizability constraint directly into the CFD solution loop, enabling early identification and rejection of unstable and non-realizable candidate models. This reduces unnecessary computational effort while guiding the search toward mathematically admissible solutions. The proposed approach achieves a 42.3% reduction in computational cost relative to the baseline CFD-driven GEP framework and reduces non-realizable models at convergence from 58.4% to 1.7%. The framework is trained on a canonical cylinder wake. The resulting models enhance mean wake prediction and remain realizable across training and test cases, with robust mean-flow transferability to diverse geometries and operating conditions, including a rectangular cylinder, an airfoil, and an axisymmetric body. The study further provides insights into realizable model statistics, coefficient trends, and their influence on wake flow predictions. These results demonstrate that incorporating realizability and stability constraints within CFD-driven learning enables efficient and mathematically admissible turbulence model discovery, offering a scalable pathway toward reliable data-driven closure development.

title: CFD driven neural network framework for latent energy storage enhancement in erythritol-based ternary hybrid nano PCM systems
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of deep winter greenhouses using passive solar heating and an underground heat storage system
abstract: Deep Winter Greenhouses (DWGs) are energy-efficient structures designed to support year-round crop production in cold climates using passive solar heating and underground heat storage systems. However, excessive heat builds up in the summer and even during the winter months. Previous studies have applied photovoltaic (PV)-powered ventilation and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling mainly to conventional greenhouse types. This study evaluated the feasibility and effectiveness of integrating a photovoltaic (PV)-powered ventilation system into DWGs using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations and techno-economic analysis across three North Central US states: Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Illinois. CFD models were developed using a tetrahedral mesh with 12.1 million elements. They were validated using field measurements collected under both summer and winter conditions. The grid convergence index between the selected and finest meshes was below 5%.. Results showed that the PV-powered ventilation system reduced crop-zone summer temperatures by 4.9 to 5.8°C under extreme conditions, providing optimal conditions for a broader range of crops. In winter, daytime temperatures remained above 6.0°C even under extreme cold conditions, while a reduced-order transient analysis indicated that nighttime temperatures fell below freezing under extreme conditions, with ventilation lowering them by only 0.8 to 1.4°C. The System Advisor Model (SAM) indicated that the PV system met the annual energy demand of 845 kWh, with a payback period under six years. By coupling CFD-derived microclimate simulations with SAM-based techno-economic evaluation, this study provides quantitative information for designing self-sustaining ventilation systems for DWGs and other cold-climate greenhouses.

title: A design of experiments–computational fluid dynamics analysis of the first hepatic artery bifurcation during transarterial radioembolization
authors: Marta Gutiérrez de San Miguel, Martín Tanco, Macarena Rodríguez-Fraile, Bruno Sangro, Raúl Antón, Jorge Aramburu
abstract: Purpose: This study investigated microsphere distribution at the first hepatic artery bifurcation during transarterial radioembolization (TARE). A combined Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Design of Experiments (DoE) methodology was developed to analyze the effect of geometric and procedural parameters, and to derive algebraic surrogate models to analyze catheter-position effects on microsphere distribution in idealized patients. Methods: First, a Central Composite Design (CCD) with a folded fractional factorial was implemented to explore an 11-variable parameter space. A total of 279 CFD simulations were performed to fit a second-order response model. Subsequently, the effect of catheter positioning was analyzed in four idealized patients through targeted CCDs. For each patient, 15 simulations were executed to develop second-order algebraic surrogate models. Results: The methodology indicated that microsphere distribution was mainly associated with flow partition and catheter coordinates. A mean discrepancy of 26 percentage points (maximum 72 percentage points) was quantified between microsphere fraction and blood flow split. While the global model served as an initial screening tool, with an adjusted R 2 = 0.54, the models for four idealized patients achieved adjusted R 2 > 0.93. These local models described the relationship between catheter position and predicted microsphere distribution, and identified regions with different levels of sensitivity to catheter position. Conclusion: The proposed CFD-DoE framework provided a structured approach to analyze microsphere distribution at the first hepatic artery bifurcation during TARE. The results indicated that microsphere distribution did not necessarily match blood flow split and that local surrogate models can describe catheter-position effects in idealized patient-specific configurations.

title: The effect of porous media, phase change materials, and hybrid PCM-liquid cooling incorporating porous copper structures on the thermal management system of lithium-ion batteries using computational fluid dynamics: advancing flow and temperature control
abstract: The accelerating adoption of electric vehicles has heightened the necessity for advanced battery thermal management systems (BTMS) to guarantee the safety, operational efficiency, and longevity of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). In this research, the effects of phase change material (PCM), copper metal foam, liquid cooling, and porous copper layers on increasing heat dissipation, temperature uniformity, and PCM effectiveness in a hybrid BTMS (HBTMS) have been numerically investigated. A 3D computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model was constructed to simulate the thermal behavior of a battery pack. The battery pack contains twelve 18650 NCM lithium-ion cells. Batteries have a discharge rate of 5C. This study investigated critical factors including liquid coolant mass flow rate, environmental temperature, inlet coolant temperature, physical properties of the porous layers, and the characteristics of the copper foam. This study investigates a hybrid battery thermal management system (BTMS) integrating phase change material (PCM) with forced convection cooling. Findings reveal that lowering the inlet coolant temperature to 293.15 K, coupled with selecting a coolant flow rate of 0.001 kg/s within the proposed hybrid configuration, achieves a favorable balance among the investigated conditions. However, it should be noted that different performance indicators—including peak temperature suppression, temperature uniformity, PCM utilization, and hydraulic performance—favor different flow rates. Therefore, the selection of coolant mass flow rate should be based on a multi-objective compromise rather than a single universal optimum. This configuration markedly decreases peak battery temperature and improves thermal uniformity compared to other conditions. Furthermore, this optimized state diminishes the liquid fraction of PCM by 70%, thereby extending its latent heat absorption capacity. Moreover, porous layers featuring elevated porosity (0.9) and 30 pores per inch (PPI) significantly boost convective heat transfer and alleviate temperature gradients within the module. The ideal copper foam design (0.9 porosity, 30 PPI) further elevates thermal regulation by accelerating the PCM phase transition and promoting more uniform heat distribution. Validation of the model against experimental results and existing literature affirms the accuracy and reliability of the simulation approach. This study underscores the promise of integrated HBTMS configurations in enhancing the thermal management, safety, and performance efficiency of LIBs deployed in high-demand applications. Beyond technical performance, a techno-economic and life-cycle analysis demonstrated that the proposed HBTMS can be realised at module-level costs of €50–90 with negligible operating electricity demand (∼€0.001–0.002 per cycle). At pack scale, levelised costs fall below €10/kWh, while extended cycle life (+25%) delivers significant value. Life-cycle assessment highlights copper and aluminium as dominant contributors to embodied GHG, but low-carbon aluminium and recycled copper strongly mitigate impacts, reinforcing the economic and environmental feasibility of the design.
